items.title: The Myth of Multitasking
items.tvi: Ảo tưởng làm nhiều việc cùng lúc
items.text:
Few claims are made with more confidence in job interviews than "I'm good at multitasking." Yet a substantial body of research suggests that, for most tasks, genuine multitasking is something the human brain is simply not built to do.
What we experience as doing two things at once is usually rapid switching between them. Each switch carries a cost: the brain must disengage from one set of rules and reload another, a process that takes a fraction of a second but adds up over a day. Studies have found that people who constantly alternate between email, messaging and a main task can take up to forty percent longer to finish, and make significantly more errors, than those who work on one thing at a time.
Perhaps more strikingly, heavy multitaskers often perform worse even when they are asked to focus on a single task. One well-known experiment found that people who habitually juggled several media streams were more easily distracted by irrelevant information, as though their capacity to filter had been weakened through lack of use.
There are exceptions. Combining a highly automatic activity, such as walking, with a demanding one, such as conversation, causes little difficulty. The problem arises when two activities compete for the same mental resources — reading and listening to speech, for instance, or writing an email during a meeting.
None of this means that modern workplaces will abandon their open-plan offices and endless notifications. But it does suggest that the most productive skill may not be the ability to do everything at once, but the discipline to do one thing properly.

qs.q: What does the writer say really happens when we 'multitask'?
qs.a: We switch quickly between tasks, which costs time
w: We use two separate parts of the brain
We complete tasks faster but less carefully
qs.why: “What we experience as doing two things at once is usually rapid switching between them. Each switch carries a cost.”

qs.q: What did the experiment suggest about habitual multitaskers?
qs.a: They became worse at ignoring distractions
w: They were better at single tasks
They could filter information more quickly
qs.why: “were more easily distracted by irrelevant information.”

qs.q: When is doing two things together NOT a problem?
qs.a: When one activity is automatic
qs.why: “Combining a highly automatic activity, such as walking, with a demanding one… causes little difficulty.”

qs.q: What is the writer's overall view?
qs.a: Focusing on one thing is more valuable than multitasking
w: Multitasking can be learned through practice
qs.why: “the most productive skill may not be the ability to do everything at once, but the discipline to do one thing properly.”

items.title: Who Owns a City's Pavements?
items.tvi: Vỉa hè thành phố thuộc về ai?
items.text:
Walk along almost any street in Hanoi and you will see the pavement put to a remarkable variety of uses: parked motorbikes, street vendors, families eating dinner on plastic stools, men playing chess, the occasional pedestrian forced to step into the road. To foreign visitors this can seem chaotic; to many residents it is simply how a city should work.
Periodic campaigns to 'reclaim the pavement' for walkers have produced mixed results. Officials argue that clear pavements are safer and make the city more attractive to tourists and investors. Critics counter that such campaigns tend to target the poorest — vendors who depend on the street for their living — while leaving untouched the cafés and car showrooms that occupy far larger areas.
Urban planners increasingly argue that the question is framed wrongly. Rather than asking whether pavements should be for walking or for trade, they suggest asking how both can coexist. Some cities have experimented with marked zones: a strip reserved for pedestrians, with vending permitted alongside it at certain hours. Others have widened pavements on busy routes while removing parking spaces, a move that is invariably unpopular with motorbike owners.
What these debates reveal is that a pavement is never just infrastructure. It reflects a society's assumptions about who has the right to public space and for what purpose. In cities where many people live in cramped homes, the street functions as an extension of the living room — and any policy that ignores this is likely to fail, however tidy it looks on paper.

qs.q: What criticism is made of 'reclaim the pavement' campaigns?
qs.a: They mainly affect poor vendors rather than big businesses
w: They make the streets more dangerous
They are too expensive to run
qs.why: “tend to target the poorest… while leaving untouched the cafés and car showrooms.”

qs.q: What do urban planners suggest?
qs.a: Finding ways for walking and trade to share space
qs.why: “they suggest asking how both can coexist.”

qs.q: Why, according to the writer, is the street like a living room for some residents?
qs.a: Their homes are very small
qs.why: “In cities where many people live in cramped homes, the street functions as an extension of the living room.”

qs.q: What does 'however tidy it looks on paper' imply?
qs.a: A plan may seem good in theory but fail in reality
w: Plans should be written more carefully
qs.why: Câu nói chính sách bỏ qua thực tế sẽ thất bại dù trên giấy trông gọn gàng.

items.title: The Value of Boredom
items.tvi: Giá trị của sự buồn chán
items.text:
Boredom has a poor reputation. We associate it with wasted time, restless children and endless meetings, and we have built an entire industry — from streaming services to infinite social media feeds — dedicated to ensuring we never have to experience it. Yet a growing number of psychologists argue that this may be a mistake.
In one frequently cited study, participants were first given a deliberately tedious task: copying numbers from a telephone directory. Afterwards, they were asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Those who had been bored came up with significantly more creative ideas than a control group who had gone straight to the second task. The researchers concluded that boredom may push the mind to search for stimulation internally, encouraging the kind of wandering thought from which original ideas emerge.
There is also a motivational dimension. Boredom, some argue, is essentially a signal that our current activity lacks meaning, prompting us to look for something more worthwhile. If we immediately silence that signal by reaching for a phone, we may never ask whether we should be doing something different with our lives.
This is not an argument for embracing tedium for its own sake. Chronic boredom, particularly in work or school, is associated with poorer performance and even health problems. The point is rather that brief, unstructured moments — waiting for a bus, lying awake, staring out of a window — may be more valuable than we assume. Filling every one of them with entertainment could, paradoxically, leave us with less to think about.

qs.q: What did the study with plastic cups suggest?
qs.a: Being bored first can increase creativity
w: Boring tasks make people less creative
qs.why: “Those who had been bored came up with significantly more creative ideas.”

qs.q: According to the 'motivational' argument, what is boredom a sign of?
qs.a: That what we are doing lacks meaning
qs.why: “Boredom… is essentially a signal that our current activity lacks meaning.”

qs.q: What does the writer say about long-term boredom?
qs.a: It can be harmful
qs.why: “Chronic boredom… is associated with poorer performance and even health problems.”

qs.q: What is the 'paradox' in the final sentence?
qs.a: Constant entertainment may reduce our thinking
w: Boredom is both good and fun
Waiting for a bus is entertaining
qs.why: “Filling every one of them with entertainment could, paradoxically, leave us with less to think about.”

items.title: Translating Poetry
items.text:
It is often said that poetry is what gets lost in translation. The remark is usually attributed to Robert Frost, although there is little evidence he ever said it, which is itself a small lesson in how ideas travel and change.
The difficulty is obvious to anyone who has tried. A poem is not simply a set of meanings; it is a particular arrangement of sounds, rhythms and associations, many of which are unique to the language in which it was written. Vietnamese, with its six tones, allows effects of musicality that English cannot reproduce. Conversely, English poets exploit rhyme and stress patterns that have no Vietnamese equivalent. A translator must therefore decide, line by line, what to sacrifice.
Some translators prioritise literal accuracy, producing versions that are faithful but often flat. Others aim to recreate the effect of the original, accepting that this may require substantial changes to its words. The poet and translator Huynh Sanh Thong, for instance, chose to render 'The Tale of Kieu' in English verse, accepting losses in precision in exchange for a work that could be read as poetry in its own right.
Critics have long debated which approach is superior, but the question may be unanswerable. Each translation is an interpretation, and a great poem can sustain many. Indeed, comparing several translations of the same work can reveal aspects of the original that no single version captures. Seen this way, translation is less a matter of loss than of multiplication: the poem survives not in one perfect copy, but in many imperfect ones.

qs.q: What point does the writer make about the Robert Frost quotation?
qs.a: It may not be his, showing how ideas change as they spread
w: It proves poetry cannot be translated
It was first written in Vietnamese
qs.why: “there is little evidence he ever said it, which is itself a small lesson in how ideas travel and change.”

qs.q: Why is poetry especially hard to translate?
qs.a: It depends on sound and associations specific to a language
w: Poets use too many rare words
qs.why: “a particular arrangement of sounds, rhythms and associations, many of which are unique to the language.”

qs.q: What did Huynh Sanh Thong accept in his translation?
qs.a: Less precision in return for a poetic English version
qs.why: “accepting losses in precision in exchange for a work that could be read as poetry in its own right.”

qs.q: What is the writer's final view of translation?
qs.a: Multiple translations together enrich our understanding
w: Only one translation can be correct
qs.why: “translation is less a matter of loss than of multiplication.”

items.title: Rewilding: Letting Nature Take Over
items.tvi: Tái hoang dã: để thiên nhiên tự phục hồi
items.text:
For much of the twentieth century, conservation meant carefully managing landscapes: cutting back vegetation, controlling animal populations and preserving particular habitats in a fixed state. Over the past two decades, an alternative philosophy known as rewilding has gained ground. Its central idea is that, given space and time, natural processes will restore damaged ecosystems more effectively than human intervention.
In practice, rewilding often involves removing barriers rather than adding things — taking down fences, allowing rivers to flood, or ending intensive farming on marginal land. In some projects, missing species are reintroduced. The return of wolves to Yellowstone National Park in the United States is the most famous example: by reducing the number of deer that grazed along riverbanks, the wolves allowed trees to recover, which in turn stabilised the banks and created habitats for birds and fish.
The approach is not without controversy. Farmers fear that predators will attack livestock, and some rural communities resent what they see as outsiders deciding the future of their land. Ecologists themselves disagree about how far 'wildness' is achievable in densely populated regions, where human influence is unavoidable.
Advocates respond that rewilding need not mean excluding people. Several projects in Europe have created jobs in eco-tourism that replace income lost from farming. The challenge, they argue, is less ecological than social: persuading communities that a landscape left partly to itself can still be a source of livelihood and pride.

qs.q: How does rewilding differ from traditional conservation?
qs.a: It relies on natural processes instead of close management
w: It focuses on protecting single species
It requires more fences and barriers
qs.why: “natural processes will restore damaged ecosystems more effectively than human intervention.”

qs.q: How did wolves help the rivers in Yellowstone?
qs.a: They reduced deer, so trees recovered along the banks
w: They ate fish that damaged the banks
They kept people away from the rivers
qs.why: “by reducing the number of deer… the wolves allowed trees to recover, which in turn stabilised the banks.”

qs.q: Why do some rural communities oppose rewilding?
qs.a: They feel others are deciding about their land
qs.why: “some rural communities resent what they see as outsiders deciding the future of their land.”

qs.q: According to advocates, what is the main challenge?
qs.a: Convincing local people of its benefits
qs.why: “The challenge… is less ecological than social: persuading communities…”

items.title: The Ethics of Tipping
items.tvi: Chuyện đạo đức của tiền boa
items.text:
Few social customs vary as widely between countries as tipping. In the United States, failing to leave around twenty percent in a restaurant is considered a serious insult, since many waiting staff depend on tips for most of their income. In Japan, by contrast, offering a tip can cause genuine confusion, as good service is regarded as part of the job rather than a favour deserving extra payment. Vietnam sits somewhere in between: tipping is not expected in most local restaurants but has become common in hotels and tourist venues.
Defenders of tipping argue that it rewards effort and gives customers a way to express appreciation. Yet research casts doubt on the idea that tips reflect service quality. Studies have found that the size of a tip is influenced far more by factors such as the weather, the size of the bill and whether the server introduced themselves by name than by how well the customer was actually served. More troublingly, several studies have found evidence that tips can be affected by the server's appearance, age or ethnicity.
Critics therefore argue that tipping shifts responsibility for fair wages from employers to customers, while exposing workers to income that is unpredictable and, at times, discriminatory. Some restaurants have experimented with 'no-tipping' policies, raising menu prices and paying staff a higher fixed wage instead. Results have been mixed: staff welcome the stability, but some customers react badly to the higher prices on the menu, even when the total cost is the same.
The persistence of tipping, in other words, may have less to do with economics than with psychology.

qs.q: Why might a tip cause confusion in Japan?
qs.a: Good service is seen as a normal part of the job
qs.why: “good service is regarded as part of the job rather than a favour deserving extra payment.”

qs.q: What does research say about tips and service quality?
qs.a: Tips depend more on other factors than on service
w: Better service always leads to bigger tips
Customers tip more in bad weather because service is slower
qs.why: “influenced far more by factors such as the weather, the size of the bill… than by how well the customer was actually served.”

qs.q: What happened in some 'no-tipping' restaurants?
qs.a: Some customers disliked higher menu prices
w: Total costs for customers rose sharply
qs.why: “some customers react badly to the higher prices on the menu, even when the total cost is the same.”

qs.q: What does the last sentence imply?
qs.a: Habits and feelings keep tipping alive, not logic
qs.why: “may have less to do with economics than with psychology.”

items.title: Why Do We Keep Things We Never Use?
items.tvi: Vì sao ta giữ đồ không bao giờ dùng?
items.text:
Open almost any cupboard and you will find them: cables for devices that no longer exist, clothes that have not fitted for years, kitchen gadgets used once and then forgotten. Most of us accept that we own too much, yet getting rid of things is surprisingly difficult. Behavioural economists offer several explanations.
The first is the so-called endowment effect: people tend to value an object more highly simply because they own it. In classic experiments, participants given a coffee mug demanded roughly twice as much to sell it as other participants were willing to pay to buy the same mug. Ownership, it seems, changes our perception of worth.
A second factor is the fear of future regret. Throwing something away closes off a possibility — the chance that we might need it one day — and the imagined pain of regretting that decision often outweighs the small, steady inconvenience of clutter. This helps explain why people keep items 'just in case' long after any realistic case has passed.
Finally, objects are often bound up with identity and memory. A worn-out jacket may represent a period of one's life; discarding it can feel like discarding part of oneself. Professional organisers report that clients frequently find it easier to let go of an item after taking a photograph of it, preserving the memory without the object.
Understanding these biases does not make decluttering painless, but it may make it more manageable. Recognising that our attachment is, at least partly, an illusion created by ownership can make the decision to let go feel less like a loss.

qs.q: What did the coffee mug experiment show?
qs.a: Owners valued the mug more than potential buyers did
w: People prefer new mugs to old ones
Buyers would pay double the shop price
qs.why: “participants given a coffee mug demanded roughly twice as much to sell it as other participants were willing to pay.”

qs.q: Why do people keep things 'just in case'?
qs.a: They fear regretting throwing them away
w: They plan to sell them later
qs.why: “the imagined pain of regretting that decision often outweighs the small, steady inconvenience of clutter.”

qs.q: Why do organisers suggest taking a photograph?
qs.a: It keeps the memory while the object goes
w: It helps sell the item online
It shows how much clutter there is
qs.why: “preserving the memory without the object.”

qs.q: What is the writer's conclusion?
qs.a: Understanding our biases can make decluttering easier
w: People should never throw things away
qs.why: “Understanding these biases does not make decluttering painless, but it may make it more manageable.”

items.title: The Rise of the Remote Village
items.text:
When high-speed internet reached the small coastal town of Quy Nhon's surrounding villages, few predicted that it would attract software developers, designers and writers from Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City. Yet over the past three years, dozens of so-called 'digital nomads' have settled there, drawn by low rents, clean air and the possibility of working for city clients while living by the sea.
Local reactions have been mixed. Guesthouse owners and café proprietors welcome the steady year-round income, which offsets the seasonal swings of tourism. Some young people who had planned to leave for the city have stayed, finding work in services that cater to the newcomers. On the other hand, rents in the most popular areas have risen sharply, and some long-term residents complain that they are being priced out of their own neighbourhoods.
There are also subtler tensions. Newcomers often keep city hours and socialise mainly with one another, creating what one resident called 'a village inside the village'. Their incomes, earned elsewhere, can be several times the local average, a disparity that is visible in everything from the cars they drive to the restaurants they frequent.
Sociologists studying similar trends elsewhere caution against simple judgements. Remote workers can revitalise declining rural economies, but the benefits are rarely shared evenly unless local authorities intervene — for instance, by protecting affordable housing or encouraging newcomers to employ local staff. Whether Quy Nhon's villages become a model of balanced growth or a cautionary tale, they suggest, will depend less on the internet than on the choices made by the people living there.

qs.q: Why do local businesses welcome the newcomers?
qs.a: They provide income throughout the year
w: They bring tourists in the summer
qs.why: “welcome the steady year-round income, which offsets the seasonal swings of tourism.”

qs.q: What problem do some long-term residents face?
qs.a: Housing has become too expensive for them
qs.why: “they are being priced out of their own neighbourhoods.”

qs.q: What does 'a village inside the village' describe?
qs.a: Newcomers living separately from locals
w: A part of the village with better internet
qs.why: “Newcomers… socialise mainly with one another.”

qs.q: According to sociologists, what will decide the outcome?
qs.a: Decisions made by local people and authorities
qs.why: “will depend less on the internet than on the choices made by the people living there.”

items.title: Can Kindness Be Taught?
items.tvi: Lòng tốt có thể dạy được không?
items.text:
In recent years, a number of schools around the world have introduced lessons designed to develop empathy — the ability to understand and share the feelings of others. Pupils discuss stories from different perspectives, practise listening without interrupting, and take part in role-plays in which they must imagine themselves in someone else's situation.
Sceptics question whether such qualities can really be taught in a classroom. Kindness, they argue, is shaped primarily by family and character, and turning it into a school subject risks reducing it to a set of correct answers that children learn to repeat. There is also concern that time spent on empathy lessons comes at the expense of academic subjects.
The evidence, however, is more encouraging than the sceptics suggest. Several large-scale studies have found that well-designed programmes reduce bullying and improve classroom behaviour, with effects that persist for years. Interestingly, some research also reports modest improvements in academic results, perhaps because pupils who feel understood are better able to concentrate.
The key word may be 'well-designed'. Programmes that rely on lectures about being nice appear to achieve little. Those that succeed tend to give children repeated opportunities to practise skills in realistic situations, and to involve teachers who model the behaviour themselves. In other words, empathy seems to be learned much like a language: not by memorising rules, but through regular use in meaningful contexts.
Whether it should be taught in schools remains a question of values as much as evidence. But the claim that it cannot be taught at all looks increasingly difficult to defend.

qs.q: What is one concern raised by sceptics?
qs.a: Children might just learn to repeat expected answers
w: Parents do not want such lessons
qs.why: “risks reducing it to a set of correct answers that children learn to repeat.”

qs.q: What possible reason is given for better academic results?
qs.a: Pupils who feel understood can concentrate better
qs.why: “perhaps because pupils who feel understood are better able to concentrate.”

qs.q: Which programmes appear to be less effective?
qs.a: Those based on lectures about being nice
w: Those where teachers model the behaviour
qs.why: “Programmes that rely on lectures about being nice appear to achieve little.”

qs.q: Why does the writer compare empathy to a language?
qs.a: Both are learned through regular practice in real situations
w: Both are taught by language teachers
qs.why: “not by memorising rules, but through regular use in meaningful contexts.”

items.title: The Hidden Cost of Free Apps
items.tvi: Cái giá ẩn của ứng dụng miễn phí
items.text:
"If you are not paying for the product, you are the product." The phrase has become a cliché, but it captures an uncomfortable truth about much of the digital economy. Many of the apps we use daily cost nothing to download because their makers earn money in other ways — chiefly by collecting data about our behaviour and selling access to it, directly or indirectly, to advertisers.
The scale of this collection is often underestimated. A single app may record not only what we search for, but where we are, how long we look at each post, and even how quickly we type. Combined with data from other sources, this information can be used to build detailed profiles that predict our interests, moods and likely purchases with considerable accuracy.
Defenders of the model point out that it has made powerful services available to billions of people who could never afford to pay for them. They also argue that most users understand and accept the bargain. Surveys, however, suggest otherwise: while people say they value their privacy, very few read privacy policies, which are typically long, vague and written in legal language.
Regulators have begun to respond. Laws in several regions now require companies to explain clearly what data they collect and to obtain meaningful consent. Some apps have introduced paid versions without advertising, giving users a genuine choice. Critics argue that these measures remain inadequate, since refusing consent often means losing access to services that have become essential to work and social life.
The question, ultimately, is not whether free apps have value — they clearly do — but whether the price we pay for them is one we would accept if it were stated openly.

qs.q: How do many free apps make money?
qs.a: By using data about users for advertising
w: By selling the app to other companies
qs.why: “by collecting data about our behaviour and selling access to it… to advertisers.”

qs.q: What do surveys suggest about users?
qs.a: They say privacy matters but rarely read the policies
w: They fully understand how data is used
qs.why: “while people say they value their privacy, very few read privacy policies.”

qs.q: Why do critics think new laws are not enough?
qs.a: Refusing consent can mean losing essential services
w: The laws are too strict for companies
qs.why: “refusing consent often means losing access to services that have become essential.”

qs.q: What is the writer's central question?
qs.a: Whether we would accept the real cost if it were made clear
qs.why: “whether the price we pay for them is one we would accept if it were stated openly.”

items.title: The Myth of the Multitasker
items.tvi: Ảo tưởng làm nhiều việc cùng lúc
items.text:
Few skills are praised as warmly in job advertisements as the ability to multitask. Candidates are expected to juggle emails, meetings and deadlines while remaining calm and efficient. Yet a substantial body of research suggests that what we call multitasking is, for most tasks, something of an illusion.
When people believe they are doing two things at once, they are usually switching rapidly between them. Each switch carries a cost: the brain must disengage from one set of rules and reload another, and during this transition both speed and accuracy suffer. The costs are small for any individual switch, which is precisely why they are easy to overlook. Accumulated over a working day, however, they can add up to a considerable loss of productive time.
More surprising is evidence about the people who multitask most. In a widely cited study, heavy media multitaskers, who regularly used several screens at once, performed worse than light multitaskers on tests requiring them to ignore irrelevant information. One might have expected practice to make them better at switching; instead, they appeared more easily distracted. Researchers are cautious about causation here. It may be that habitual multitasking weakens attention, or that people who are already easily distracted are drawn to it.
None of this means that combining activities is always harmful. Listening to music while running, or chatting while cooking a familiar dish, causes little difficulty, because at least one task has become automatic. Problems arise when two tasks compete for the same mental resources, as when we try to write a report while following a conversation.
Some organisations have begun to respond. They encourage "focus time", blocks of the day free from meetings and notifications, and discourage the expectation that messages be answered within minutes. Advocates argue that such measures improve both the quality of work and employee wellbeing. Critics counter that in fast-moving industries responsiveness is itself part of the job, and that a culture of protected concentration may suit some roles better than others.
What seems clear is that the celebrated multitasker owes much of that reputation to appearances. Looking busy and being effective are not the same thing, and an office full of people answering messages during meetings may be less productive than it seems.

qs.q: What is the writer's main point in the first paragraph?
qs.a: The popular idea of multitasking is largely mistaken
w: Multitasking is easy to learn with practice
Most jobs no longer require multitasking
qs.why: “what we call multitasking is, for most tasks, something of an illusion.”

qs.q: Why are the costs of switching between tasks “easy to overlook”?
qs.a: Each individual cost is very small
w: They occur only at the end of the day
qs.why: “The costs are small for any individual switch, which is precisely why they are easy to overlook.”

qs.q: What was surprising about heavy media multitaskers in the study?
qs.a: They were worse at ignoring irrelevant information
w: They switched between tasks faster than others
They used fewer screens than expected
They performed better on memory tests
qs.why: “performed worse than light multitaskers on tests requiring them to ignore irrelevant information.”

qs.q: Why are researchers “cautious about causation”?
qs.a: It is unclear whether multitasking causes distraction or the reverse
w: The study included too few participants
qs.why: “It may be that habitual multitasking weakens attention, or that people who are already easily distracted are drawn to it.”

qs.q: According to the writer, combining two activities is least problematic when
qs.a: one of them requires little conscious attention
qs.why: “at least one task has become automatic.”

qs.q: What does the writer imply in the final paragraph?
qs.a: Appearing busy can be mistaken for being productive
w: Meetings should be banned in offices
Messages should never be answered during work
qs.why: “Looking busy and being effective are not the same thing.”

items.title: Who Owns a Recipe?
items.tvi: Công thức nấu ăn thuộc về ai?
items.text:
In most countries, you cannot copyright a recipe. A list of ingredients is regarded as a set of facts, and a method for combining them is considered too functional to qualify as creative expression. A chef can spend years perfecting a dish, only to see it reproduced, down to the last spoonful of fish sauce, in a rival restaurant across the street.
At first glance, this seems unjust. We protect novels, songs and software, so why not culinary creativity? Yet many chefs are surprisingly relaxed about the situation, and some legal scholars argue that the absence of protection has actually benefited cooking. Because ideas circulate freely, dishes evolve rapidly: a technique invented in one kitchen is adapted, improved and reinterpreted in dozens of others. Had every innovation been locked behind legal barriers, the argument goes, the culinary world would be far less inventive.
This does not mean that the profession operates without rules. Researchers who interviewed leading chefs found a set of informal norms that function almost like law. Copying a signature dish exactly is widely regarded as unacceptable; borrowing an idea without acknowledging its source can damage a chef's reputation; and passing on a colleague's secret technique without permission may lead to exclusion from professional networks. Because the world of high-end cooking is relatively small, reputation acts as a powerful enforcement mechanism.
The system has its weaknesses. Informal norms work best within close-knit communities and are far less effective when large food companies are involved. A small family restaurant may find its best-known dish copied by a chain with the resources to market it nationally, and have no realistic means of responding. Similar concerns arise when traditional dishes from particular regions or communities are commercialised by outsiders who neither credit nor compensate their originators.
Some have proposed new forms of protection, such as geographical labels for traditional dishes, similar to those that already exist for certain cheeses and wines. Others fear that such measures would freeze recipes in time and restrict the borrowing that has always driven food culture. Between theft and inspiration lies a grey area that no law is likely to define precisely, which may be why cooks have relied for so long on a code of honour rather than on the courts.

qs.q: Why are recipes generally not protected by copyright?
qs.a: They are seen as factual and functional rather than creative
w: Chefs have never asked for protection
They are too difficult to define legally
qs.why: “regarded as a set of facts… too functional to qualify as creative expression.”

qs.q: What argument do some legal scholars make?
qs.a: Lack of protection has encouraged innovation in cooking
w: Chefs should be paid when their recipes are copied
Recipes are more creative than novels
Copying has damaged the restaurant industry
qs.why: “the absence of protection has actually benefited cooking… dishes evolve rapidly.”

qs.q: What do the researchers' interviews reveal?
qs.a: Chefs follow unwritten rules about copying
w: Most chefs copy each other's dishes exactly
Chefs regularly take each other to court
Chefs keep all their techniques secret
qs.why: “a set of informal norms that function almost like law.”

qs.q: Why is reputation effective in enforcing these norms?
qs.a: The community of top chefs is small
w: Chefs are legally required to credit others
qs.why: “Because the world of high-end cooking is relatively small, reputation acts as a powerful enforcement mechanism.”

qs.q: What weakness of the informal system does the writer identify?
qs.a: It offers little protection against large companies
w: It is too strict for young chefs
It prevents traditional dishes from being sold
It is not understood by most chefs
qs.why: “far less effective when large food companies are involved.”

qs.q: How does the writer seem to view proposals for geographical labels?
qs.a: As having both advantages and possible disadvantages
w: As already successful for all dishes
qs.why: Nêu đề xuất bảo hộ rồi nêu lo ngại “freeze recipes in time”: cân nhắc hai mặt.

items.title: The Value of Boredom
items.tvi: Giá trị của sự buồn chán
items.text:
Boredom has a poor reputation. It is associated with wasted time, restless children and unproductive afternoons, and an entire industry of apps, streaming services and notifications exists to make sure we never have to experience it. Yet a growing number of psychologists argue that boredom serves a purpose, and that our determination to eliminate it may come at a price.
According to one influential view, boredom is a signal, much like hunger or pain. It tells us that our current activity is not meeting our needs and prompts us to look for something more meaningful. Seen this way, the problem is not boredom itself but what we do in response. If every moment of emptiness is immediately filled by a phone, the signal is silenced before it can lead anywhere.
Some studies have explored a possible link between boredom and creativity. In one experiment, participants who first completed a deliberately tedious task, such as copying numbers from a telephone directory, later produced more original ideas in a creative thinking test than those who had not. The researchers suggested that a bored mind tends to wander, and that mind-wandering allows unexpected connections to form. Other researchers have been more cautious, noting that the effects in such studies are often small and not always replicated.
There are also important distinctions to be made. Occasional boredom, which a person is free to respond to, appears very different from chronic boredom, which has been associated with depression, risky behaviour and poor performance at work and school. Advocates of boredom are not suggesting that people should be trapped in monotonous situations; rather, they argue that brief periods of unstructured time can be valuable.
This raises questions for parents and teachers in particular. Children whose every hour is scheduled with lessons, activities and screens may have few opportunities to discover what interests them on their own. Several educators now recommend allowing children some unplanned time, even if they complain. The discomfort, they suggest, is often the first step towards inventing a game, starting a project or simply noticing the world.
None of this makes boredom pleasant. But it may be worth tolerating it for a little longer before reaching for the nearest screen.

qs.q: What does the writer say about the apps and services mentioned in paragraph 1?
qs.a: They are designed to stop people from feeling bored
w: They were created to improve productivity
qs.why: “an entire industry… exists to make sure we never have to experience it.”

qs.q: In the “signal” view, why is boredom compared to hunger or pain?
qs.a: It tells us that something needs to change
w: It disappears if we ignore it
qs.why: “It tells us that our current activity is not meeting our needs and prompts us to look for something more meaningful.”

qs.q: What was found in the experiment with the telephone directory?
qs.a: Participants who had done a dull task later had more original ideas
w: All participants found the task enjoyable
qs.why: “later produced more original ideas in a creative thinking test.”

qs.q: Why are some researchers “more cautious”?
qs.a: The results are often weak and not always repeated
qs.why: “the effects in such studies are often small and not always replicated.”

qs.q: What distinction does the writer draw in paragraph 4?
qs.a: Short, occasional boredom differs from long-term boredom
w: Boredom at work differs from boredom at school
Children feel boredom more than adults
qs.why: “Occasional boredom… appears very different from chronic boredom.”

qs.q: What is the writer's overall position?
qs.a: People could benefit from accepting some boredom
w: Boredom should be eliminated from children's lives
Screens are the main cause of depression
qs.why: “it may be worth tolerating it for a little longer before reaching for the nearest screen.”

items.title: Rewilding: Letting Nature Take Over
items.tvi: Tái hoang dã: để thiên nhiên tự phục hồi
items.text:
For much of the twentieth century, conservation meant protecting particular species or managing landscapes to look a certain way: cutting grass, removing unwanted plants and controlling animal numbers. In recent years, a different approach has gained ground. Known as rewilding, it involves stepping back and allowing natural processes to shape the land, sometimes with the help of reintroduced species that have disappeared from an area.
One of the most frequently cited examples comes from a large estate in southern England, where the owners gave up intensive farming in the early 2000s. Instead of planting crops, they let the fields be grazed by free-roaming herds of cattle, ponies and pigs, chosen to imitate the role once played by wild animals. Within two decades, the estate had become home to several species that are rare elsewhere in the country, including nightingales and purple emperor butterflies. The transformation was not planned in detail; it emerged from the interaction of plants and animals.
Supporters argue that rewilding is both cheaper and more effective than traditional conservation, because nature does much of the work itself. They also point to wider benefits: restored wetlands can reduce flooding, and growing forests store carbon. Visitors drawn by wildlife can bring income to rural communities.
The approach is not without critics, however. Farmers sometimes see rewilding as a threat to their livelihoods and to food production, particularly when productive land is taken out of use. Reintroducing large predators, such as wolves or lynx, provokes fierce debate wherever it is proposed, since such animals may attack livestock. Some ecologists also warn that "letting nature decide" is less straightforward than it sounds, as landscapes everywhere have been shaped by humans for thousands of years and there is no single natural state to return to.
Perhaps the most useful lesson from the debate is that rewilding works best when local people are involved from the start. Projects imposed from outside, however good their intentions, often meet resistance, while those that share decisions and benefits with nearby communities tend to last. Nature may be able to look after itself, but people still need to be persuaded to let it.

qs.q: How does rewilding differ from earlier conservation?
qs.a: It allows natural processes to shape the land with less human control
w: It focuses on protecting single species
It keeps landscapes looking the same
It removes all animals from an area
qs.why: “stepping back and allowing natural processes to shape the land.”

qs.q: Why were cattle, ponies and pigs used on the English estate?
qs.a: To play a role similar to that of wild animals
qs.why: “chosen to imitate the role once played by wild animals.”

qs.q: What does the writer emphasise about the estate's transformation?
qs.a: It happened without a detailed plan
w: It was carefully designed by scientists
It was paid for by the government
It took more than fifty years
qs.why: “The transformation was not planned in detail; it emerged from the interaction of plants and animals.”

qs.q: Which benefit of rewilding is NOT mentioned?
qs.a: Higher crop yields for farmers
qs.why: Bài nhắc giảm lũ, lưu trữ carbon, thu nhập từ khách; không nói tăng sản lượng mùa màng (nông dân còn lo mất đất).

qs.q: Why do some ecologists say “letting nature decide” is not straightforward?
qs.a: Human influence makes it hard to define a natural state
qs.why: “landscapes… have been shaped by humans for thousands of years and there is no single natural state to return to.”

qs.q: What does the final sentence suggest?
qs.a: Success depends on winning people's support
w: Nature does not need human help at all
People should not live near rewilded areas
Rewilding projects should be kept secret
qs.why: “Nature may be able to look after itself, but people still need to be persuaded to let it.”

items.title: Should We Trust Online Reviews?
items.tvi: Có nên tin nhận xét trên mạng?
items.text:
Before booking a hotel, choosing a restaurant or buying a kettle, most of us now consult the opinions of strangers. Online reviews have become one of the most influential forces in modern consumer life, and their appeal is easy to understand. Unlike advertising, they seem to offer the honest views of ordinary people with no reason to deceive.
That assumption, unfortunately, is not always justified. Fake reviews, written by businesses about themselves or by paid agencies, are a persistent problem, and investigations have repeatedly uncovered networks offering five-star ratings for a fee. Some sellers offer refunds or free products to customers who leave positive comments, a practice that is banned on many platforms but difficult to detect.
Even genuine reviews present a distorted picture. People are far more likely to write a review after an unusually good or unusually bad experience than after an ordinary one, so ratings tend to cluster at the extremes. Early reviews also carry disproportionate weight: a product that receives a few enthusiastic comments in its first weeks may attract more buyers, who in turn leave more positive reviews, regardless of whether it is genuinely better than its competitors.
There is, moreover, the question of what a rating actually measures. A one-star review of a restaurant may reflect a long wait on a busy evening, a misunderstanding about the menu, or simply a bad mood. Researchers who analysed thousands of hotel reviews found that a substantial share of negative comments concerned factors outside the hotel's control, such as the weather or noisy neighbours.
Platforms have responded with verification systems and algorithms designed to identify suspicious patterns, and in some countries regulators have begun to fine companies that publish fake reviews. These measures help, but they are unlikely to solve the problem entirely, because the incentives to manipulate ratings remain strong.
For consumers, the sensible approach is neither blind trust nor complete cynicism. Reading a range of reviews, paying attention to specific details rather than star ratings, and treating both extremes with some suspicion can help separate useful information from noise. Reviews, in other words, are best read the way one might listen to advice from a crowd: worth hearing, but not to be followed without thinking.

qs.q: Why, according to the writer, do people find online reviews appealing?
qs.a: They seem more honest than advertising
w: They are always up to date
They are checked by the government
qs.why: “Unlike advertising, they seem to offer the honest views of ordinary people with no reason to deceive.”

qs.q: Why do ratings tend to “cluster at the extremes”?
qs.a: People mostly write reviews after very good or very bad experiences
w: Most products are either excellent or terrible
Customers are paid to give extreme ratings
qs.why: “far more likely to write a review after an unusually good or unusually bad experience.”

qs.q: What problem with early reviews is described?
qs.a: They can influence later sales and ratings too strongly
w: They are usually written by the seller
They are often deleted by platforms
They are less detailed than later reviews
qs.why: “Early reviews also carry disproportionate weight… regardless of whether it is genuinely better.”

qs.q: What did the analysis of hotel reviews show?
qs.a: Many complaints concerned things hotels could not control
qs.why: “a substantial share of negative comments concerned factors outside the hotel's control.”

qs.q: Why does the writer think platform measures will not solve the problem completely?
qs.a: There are still strong reasons for businesses to cheat
qs.why: “because the incentives to manipulate ratings remain strong.”

qs.q: What does the comparison with “advice from a crowd” suggest?
qs.a: Reviews should be considered critically, not simply obeyed
w: Popular products are always the best
qs.why: “worth hearing, but not to be followed without thinking.”
